# Virtual environments {#sec-ch-venv}

> *"It works on my machine."* — every developer, at least once. Virtual
> environments exist so that you never have to say it again.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- explain the problem virtual environments solve (conflicting dependencies,
  reproducibility) and **how** `venv` works inside (`pyvenv.cfg`,
  `sys.prefix`);
- create, activate, use, deactivate and remove a virtual environment with
  `venv` (and `virtualenv`);
- use a virtual environment as a **Jupyter kernel**;
- create environments for a **specific Python version**;
- **share** a project so that anyone can recreate its environment, and know
  when to reach for lock files, conda or containers;
- get started with the three tools of the next courses — **NumPy**,
  **pandas** and **Matplotlib** — in the optional crash course at the end.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
Creating, using and removing virtual environments; using them in Jupyter; choosing the Python version; sharing projects; a primer on NumPy, pandas and Matplotlib.
:::

## Intuition: one kitchen per recipe

Imagine a single kitchen shared by every recipe you cook: one recipe wants the
oven at 180 °C, another at 250 °C, at the same time. That is a single global
Python installation shared by all your projects: project A needs `pandas 1.5`,
project B needs `pandas 2.2`, and `site-packages` can hold only one of them.
Upgrading for B silently breaks A.

A **virtual environment** gives each project **its own kitchen**: its own
`site-packages`, with its own versions, while sharing the same Python
interpreter. Environments are cheap (a folder), disposable (delete the folder)
and reproducible (a `requirements.txt` recreates one exactly,
@sec-requirements).

## How `venv` works {#sec-venv-internals}

The `venv` module was added in Python 3.3 by PEP 405 [@pep405], standardising
ideas from the earlier third-party tool **virtualenv** (Ian Bicking, 2007).
`python -m venv .venv` creates a directory:

```text
.venv/
├── pyvenv.cfg              ← "home = <path of the base Python>", version, options
├── bin/        (Scripts\ on Windows)
│   ├── python  → link (or copy) of the base interpreter
│   ├── pip
│   └── activate            ← shell script that edits PATH and the prompt
└── lib/python3.13/site-packages/    ← this environment's own packages
```

The mechanism is simple and elegant [@pep405]: when the Python interpreter
starts, it looks for a file named `pyvenv.cfg` **next to its executable or one
directory above**. If it finds one, it sets `sys.prefix` to the environment's
directory (while `sys.base_prefix` still points to the base installation), and
therefore puts the **environment's** `site-packages` on `sys.path` instead of
the global one. Nothing else is needed. In particular, **"activating" is only a
convenience**: it prepends `.venv/bin` to the `PATH` so that typing `python` or
`pip` finds the environment's executables first. Running `.venv/bin/python`
directly works just as well.

::: {.deep}
## Verifying how `venv` works, from Python

Let us verify all of this by creating an environment from Python (without pip,
so that no network is needed):

```{python}
import venv, subprocess, sys, tempfile
from pathlib import Path

env_dir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / ".venv"
venv.create(env_dir, with_pip=False)                # same as: python -m venv --without-pip .venv
env_python = env_dir / ("Scripts/python.exe" if sys.platform == "win32" else "bin/python")

print(sorted(p.name for p in env_dir.iterdir()))
cfg = (env_dir / "pyvenv.cfg").read_text().splitlines()
print([line.split(" = ")[0] for line in cfg])       # the keys stored in pyvenv.cfg

probe = ("import sys; print('in venv:', sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix); "
         "print('site-packages:', [p.split('/')[-4:] for p in sys.path if p.endswith('site-packages')])")
print(subprocess.run([str(env_python), "-c", probe], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout)
print("this kernel in a venv?", sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)
```

The test `sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix` is the official way for a program to
know whether it runs inside a virtual environment.
:::


## Creating, using and removing an environment {#sec-venv-commands}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### macOS / Linux

```bash
cd my-project
python3 -m venv .venv               # create (".venv" is the conventional name)
source .venv/bin/activate           # activate: the prompt shows (.venv)
python -m pip install pandas        # installs into .venv only
python -m pip list                  # only this environment's packages
deactivate                          # leave the environment
rm -rf .venv                        # remove it: it is just a folder
```

### Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
cd my-project
py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1          # if blocked: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
python -m pip install pandas
deactivate
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force .venv
```

:::

Good practices:

- **one environment per project**, created inside the project folder;
- **never commit** the environment folder to Git: add `.venv/` to
  `.gitignore` (it contains machine-specific paths and binaries); commit the
  `requirements.txt` instead;
- environments are **not relocatable**: if you move or rename the project
  folder, delete and recreate the environment;
- `virtualenv` (`pip install virtualenv; virtualenv .venv`) is a faster
  third-party alternative with the same layout; `uv venv` is a newer, very fast
  one.

## Using an environment with Jupyter {#sec-venv-jupyter}

Jupyter runs code in a **kernel** (@sec-dev-environment), and a kernel is a
specific Python interpreter. To use your environment's packages in a notebook,
**register the environment as a kernel**:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate                     # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install ipykernel
python -m ipykernel install --user --name my-project --display-name "Python (my-project)"
jupyter kernelspec list                       # shows the registered kernels
```

This writes a small `kernel.json` file whose `argv` points to
`.venv/bin/python`; in Jupyter (or VS Code) choose *Kernel → Change kernel →
Python (my-project)*. Inside a notebook, check which interpreter you are using
with `import sys; sys.executable`, and install packages with `%pip install …`,
which always targets the running kernel. Remove a kernel with
`jupyter kernelspec uninstall my-project`.

**Google Colab** is different: each notebook runs in a fresh, pre-configured
cloud machine. You do not create virtual environments there; you install
missing packages with `%pip install` at the top of the notebook, and they last
until the runtime is recycled.

## Choosing the Python version {#sec-python-versions}

A virtual environment uses the interpreter that created it: **the Python
version is fixed at creation time**. To create an environment for another
version, invoke that version's interpreter:

```bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv          # macOS/Linux, if python3.12 is installed
py -3.12 -m venv .venv            # Windows: the py launcher selects installed versions (py --list)
```

To install several Python versions side by side use the official installers,
your system's package manager, **pyenv** (macOS/Linux), or `uv python install
3.12`. Declare the versions your project supports in `pyproject.toml`
(`requires-python = ">=3.10"`, @sec-real-package) and document the one you
used. Each Python release is supported for five years; check the status page
before choosing [@pythonversions].

## Sharing a project {#sec-sharing-projects}

To let someone else (or yourself in six months, or a grader) run your project:

1. work in a clean virtual environment;
2. export the dependencies: `python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt`
   (@sec-requirements), or better maintain direct dependencies by hand and
   generate a lock file;
3. commit code, `requirements.txt` (or `pyproject.toml` + lock file) and a
   `README` with the **exact setup commands** — but not `.venv/`;
4. the recipient runs:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/<user>/<project>.git
cd <project>
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python main.py
```

Levels of reproducibility, from weakest to strongest:

| Mechanism | Pins | Does not pin |
|---|---|---|
| `requirements.txt` with ranges | direct dependencies, loosely | transitive deps, Python, OS |
| `pip freeze` / lock file | all Python packages, exactly (with hashes: byte-for-byte) | Python version, system libraries |
| **conda** environment (`environment.yml`) | also Python itself and non-Python libraries (CUDA, MKL) | the OS |
| **container** (Docker image) | the whole user-space system | the hardware and kernel |

For data science and deep learning, conda (or its fast re-implementation
mamba) is popular because packages such as PyTorch with GPU support depend on
compiled non-Python libraries; containers are the standard for deploying
models to production.

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The phone book needs no third-party packages and is
delivered on Colab, so no virtual environment is required. If you develop it
locally (e.g. in VS Code, turning it into the package of @sec-real-package),
create a `.venv`, register it as a Jupyter kernel to run the notebook with the
same interpreter, and ship a `README` with the commands above — the habit you
will need from the next project on, when NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn and
PyTorch enter the scene.
:::

## Optional crash course: NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib {#sec-crash-courses}

The next courses rely on three libraries. The master offers optional crash
courses on them; this section gives you the essential concepts, with the
mathematics behind them, so that the next parts of the book can build on them.
(Each library will be studied in depth where it is used.)

### NumPy: arrays and vectorised computation {#sec-numpy}

**NumPy** [@harris2020] provides the **`ndarray`**: an $n$-dimensional array of
elements **of one type** (`dtype`) stored **contiguously** in memory. Unlike a
list of Python objects (@sec-dynamic-arrays), the elements are raw machine
numbers, so operations run in compiled C loops — **vectorisation** — typically
10–100× faster than Python loops.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import time

a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
M = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)          # 3 rows, 4 columns
print(a.dtype, a.shape, M.shape, M.ndim, M.size)
print(M[1, 2], M[:, 0], M[0, ::2])       # indexing and slicing in each dimension
print(a * 2, a + a, a ** 2, np.sqrt(a))  # element-wise operations: no loops
print(M.sum(), M.sum(axis=0), M.mean(axis=1))   # reductions along an axis

x = np.random.default_rng(0).random(1_000_000)
t0 = time.perf_counter(); s1 = sum(v * v for v in x); t1 = time.perf_counter()
s2 = float(np.dot(x, x)); t2 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"python loop {t1 - t0:.3f} s, numpy {t2 - t1:.5f} s, same result: {np.isclose(s1, s2)}")
```

**Broadcasting.** Element-wise operations between arrays of different shapes
follow one rule [@harris2020]: compare the shapes from the **last** dimension
backwards; two dimensions are compatible if they are **equal or one of them is
1**; missing leading dimensions count as 1; a dimension of size 1 is
(virtually) repeated to match the other.

```{python}
col = np.array([[0], [10], [20]])        # shape (3, 1)
row = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])             # shape (4,)  -> treated as (1, 4)
print((col + row).shape)                 # (3, 4)
print(col + row)
```

**Linear algebra.** The two products you will meet in every model:

- **dot product** of $u, v\in\mathbb{R}^n$: $u\cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i$
  (`u @ v`), costing $n$ multiplications;
- **matrix product** of $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and
  $B\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$:
  $$
  (AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ik}B_{kj}, \qquad 1\le i\le m,\ 1\le j\le p,
  $$ {#eq-matmul}
  i.e. entry $(i,j)$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of
  $B$. It costs $mnp$ multiplications ($n^3$ for square matrices) with the
  definition — the reason GPUs, which do thousands of multiplications in
  parallel, power deep learning.

::: {.deep}
## Properties of the matrix product, and why the order of multiplication matters

::: {#thm-matmul-assoc}
## The matrix product is associative but not commutative
For conformable matrices, $(AB)C = A(BC)$; in general $AB \ne BA$.
:::

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-matmul-assoc
By @eq-matmul twice,
$$
\big((AB)C\big)_{ij} = \sum_{l} (AB)_{il}C_{lj} = \sum_l\sum_k A_{ik}B_{kl}C_{lj}
= \sum_k A_{ik}\sum_l B_{kl}C_{lj} = \sum_k A_{ik}(BC)_{kj} = \big(A(BC)\big)_{ij},
$$
exchanging two finite sums. For non-commutativity one counterexample suffices:
with $A = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and
$B = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
$AB = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ but
$BA = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. $\blacksquare$
:::

Associativity has a practical side: $(AB)C$ and $A(BC)$ give the same result
but can cost very differently. With $A$ of shape $1000\times2$, $B$ of
$2\times1000$, $C$ of $1000\times 1$: $(AB)C$ costs
$1000\cdot2\cdot1000 + 1000\cdot1000\cdot1 = 3\times10^6$ multiplications,
$A(BC)$ only $2\cdot1000\cdot1 + 1000\cdot2\cdot1 = 4000$.

```{python}
A = np.array([[0, 1], [0, 0]]); B = np.array([[0, 0], [1, 0]])
print(A @ B, B @ A, sep="\n")
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
A, B, C = rng.random((1000, 2)), rng.random((2, 1000)), rng.random((1000, 1))
print(np.allclose((A @ B) @ C, A @ (B @ C)))
S = np.array([[3.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]]); y = np.array([9.0, 8.0])
print(np.linalg.solve(S, y))              # solve the linear system S x = y
```
:::


### pandas: tables of data {#sec-pandas}

**pandas** [@mckinney2010] provides the **`DataFrame`**: a table with labelled
columns of possibly different types (each column is a NumPy-backed
**`Series`**), plus tools to read, clean, filter, group and aggregate data. It
is the in-memory equivalent of a spreadsheet or SQL table, and it reads the
CSV/JSON files of @sec-ch-files directly.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

csv_text = """name,city,age,spend
Ada,London,36,120.5
Alan,Manchester,41,80.0
Grace,New York,85,200.0
Linus,Helsinki,28,
Anna,London,30,60.0
"""
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv_text))          # pd.read_csv("file.csv") for a real file
print(df.shape, list(df.columns), df.dtypes.to_dict())
print(df.head(3))
print(df[df["age"] < 40][["name", "spend"]])  # filter rows, select columns
print(df["spend"].isna().sum(), "missing value(s); mean spend:", round(df["spend"].mean(), 2))
print(df.groupby("city")["spend"].agg(["count", "mean"]))
print(df.describe().loc[["mean", "std"]])
```

`describe()` reports, among others, the **mean**
$\bar x = \frac1n\sum_i x_i$ and the **sample standard deviation**
$s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}$ (with $n-1$, *Bessel's
correction*, which makes $s^2$ an unbiased estimator of the variance; we will
prove it in the statistics part of the book). Two identities used constantly
are worth proving now:

::: {.deep}
## Two identities for the mean and the variance

::: {#prp-variance-identity}
## Two identities for the mean and the variance
For numbers $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with mean $\bar x$: (a)
$\sum_i (x_i - \bar x) = 0$; (b)
$\frac1n\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2 = \frac1n\sum_i x_i^2 - \bar x^{\,2}$.
:::

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-variance-identity
(a) $\sum_i(x_i - \bar x) = \sum_i x_i - n\bar x = n\bar x - n\bar x = 0$.
(b) Expanding the square,
$\frac1n\sum_i (x_i^2 - 2x_i\bar x + \bar x^2) = \frac1n\sum_i x_i^2 - 2\bar x\cdot\frac1n\sum_i x_i + \bar x^2 = \frac1n\sum_i x_i^2 - 2\bar x^2 + \bar x^2$.
$\blacksquare$ (Numerically, formula (b) suffers from cancellation when the
variance is small compared with the mean, cf. @thm-sum-error; libraries use
the two-pass formula or Welford's algorithm [@welford1962].)
:::
:::


### Matplotlib: plotting {#sec-matplotlib}

**Matplotlib** [@hunter2007] is the standard plotting library. Its
object-oriented interface: a **Figure** contains one or more **Axes**
(plots); you call plotting methods on the axes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-crash-matplotlib
#| fig-cap: "A first Matplotlib figure: a line plot of three growth functions (left) and a histogram of 10,000 normal samples (right)."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

n = np.arange(1, 21)
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))
ax1.plot(n, n, label="n")
ax1.plot(n, n * np.log2(n), label="n log n")
ax1.plot(n, n ** 2, label="n²")
ax1.set_xlabel("n"); ax1.set_ylabel("operations"); ax1.set_title("Growth rates")
ax1.legend()
samples = np.random.default_rng(42).normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=10_000)
ax2.hist(samples, bins=40, color="tab:green", alpha=0.8)
ax2.set_title("Normal samples"); ax2.set_xlabel("value")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Use `fig.savefig("plot.png", dpi=150)` to save a figure to a file. In the
data-analysis part of the book we will study which chart fits which question.

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Forgetting to activate** (or to select the kernel) and installing into the
  wrong environment: check `sys.executable` / `which python`.
- **Committing `.venv/`** to Git.
- **Moving the project folder**: recreate the environment.
- **Mixing conda and pip** carelessly in the same environment: install with
  conda first, then pip, and record both.
- **A notebook kernel that is not the environment** you installed packages
  into: `%pip install` in the notebook avoids it.
- **NumPy integer overflow** (@sec-twos-complement) and **shape mismatches**:
  print `.dtype` and `.shape` when in doubt.
:::

## Summary

- A virtual environment is a folder with its own `site-packages`;
  `pyvenv.cfg` makes the interpreter set `sys.prefix` to it; activation just
  edits `PATH`.
- Create with `python -m venv .venv`, activate, install, `deactivate`, delete
  the folder to remove; one environment per project, never committed.
- Register environments as Jupyter kernels with `ipykernel`; on Colab use
  `%pip`.
- The Python version is fixed at creation; choose it with `python3.X` / `py
  -3.X` / pyenv / uv.
- Share with `requirements.txt` or lock files plus a README; conda and
  containers pin more of the stack.
- NumPy (arrays, broadcasting, linear algebra), pandas (DataFrames) and
  Matplotlib (figures and axes) are the tools of the next courses.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ch13-check}
Write a script that prints whether it runs inside a virtual environment, the
path of the interpreter, and the list of installed distributions with their
versions (use `importlib.metadata.distributions()`).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```python
import sys
from importlib.metadata import distributions
print("venv:", sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix, "| interpreter:", sys.executable)
for d in sorted(distributions(), key=lambda d: d.metadata["Name"].lower()):
    print(d.metadata["Name"], d.version)
```
:::

::: {#exr-ch13-broadcast}
Predict the shapes (or the error) of `A + B` for: `(5, 3)` and `(3,)`;
`(5, 3)` and `(5,)`; `(4, 1, 3)` and `(2, 1)`; `(2, 3)` and `(3, 2)`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
`(5, 3)`; error (last dimensions 3 vs 5); `(4, 2, 3)`; error (3 vs 2).
:::

::: {#exr-ch13-chain}
Matrices $A_1$ ($10\times100$), $A_2$ ($100\times5$), $A_3$ ($5\times50$). Which
parenthesisation of $A_1A_2A_3$ needs fewer multiplications? (This is the
*matrix-chain* problem, solved in general by dynamic programming.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$(A_1A_2)A_3$: $10\cdot100\cdot5 + 10\cdot5\cdot50 = 5000 + 2500 = 7500$.
$A_1(A_2A_3)$: $100\cdot5\cdot50 + 10\cdot100\cdot50 = 25000 + 50000 = 75000$.
The first is ten times cheaper [@cormen2022, §14.2].
:::
